nodes.raw_latex:
Let $S$ be a cardinal.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
An $S$-sorted type is a tuple $(F,\mathrm{ar},{\rm dom},{\rm cod})$ that satisfies the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$F$ is a set.
\item
$\mathrm{ar}:F\rightarrow {\rm Card}$, where ${\rm Card}$ is the class of all cardinals.
\item
${\rm dom},{\rm cod}$ are functions defined on $F$ and satisfy
${\rm dom}(f):\mathrm{ar}(f)\rightarrow S$, ${\rm cod}(f)\in S$
for each $f\in F$.
\end{itemize}
\item
For an $S$-sorted type $F$, $F$-algebra is a pair $(A,\tau)$
that satisfies the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ is an $S$-indexed family of sets.
\item
$\tau$ is a function defined on $F$ and
$\tau(f)$ is a mapping $\prod_{i\in\mathrm{ar}(f)}A_{{\rm dom}(f)(i)}\rightarrow A_{{\rm cod}(f)}$
for each $f\in F$.
\end{itemize}
\item
For an infinite cardinal $\kappa$, $F$ is said $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary if
$\mathrm{ar}(f)<\kappa$ hold for all $f\in F$.
\item
The height of $F$ is defined as
\[
\mathrm{Ht}(F):=
\begin{cases}
\omega_0& \text{if }F\text{ is finitary},\\
\min\{\kappa\in\mathrm{Ord}\mid {\rm cf}(\kappa) >\mathrm{ar}(f)\text{ for all }f\in F\}& \text{ if }F\text{ is infinitary},
\end{cases}
\]
where $\omega_0$ is the minimum infinite ordinal,
$\mathrm{Ord}$ is the class of all ordinals, and ${\rm cf}(\kappa)$ is
the cofinality of $\kappa$, i.e., the minimum cardinal $\alpha$
such that there exists an $\alpha$-indexed family $(\lambda_i)_{i\in\alpha}$
of cardinals that satisfies $\lambda_i<\kappa$ (for all $i\in\alpha$) and
$\sup_{i\in\alpha} \lambda_i=\kappa$.
\item
For an $S$-sorted type $F$, an ordinal $\alpha$, a cardinal $\lambda$,
a mapping $v:\lambda\rightarrow S$ and an element $s\in S$,
the set $T_{\alpha,(\lambda,v,s)}$ of all $(\lambda,v)$-ary $s$-valued terms of $F$
with complexity less than $\alpha$
is inductively defined as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$T_{0,(\lambda,v,s)}:=\{x_i\mid v(i)=s,i\in\lambda\}$.
(The set of variable symbols.)
\item
$T_{\alpha+1,(\lambda,v,s)}:=T_{\alpha,(\lambda,v,s)}\cup
\{(f,(t_i)_{i\in \mathrm{ar}(F)})\mid 
 f\in F,t_i\in T_{\alpha,(\lambda,v,{\rm dom}(f)(i))},{\rm cod}(f)=s\}$.
\item
$T_{\alpha,(\lambda,v,s)}:=\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha} T_{\beta,(\lambda,v,s)}$
if $\alpha$ is a limit ordinal.
\end{itemize}
The set of all $(\lambda,v)$-ary $s$-valued terms of $F$ is $T_{\mathrm{Ht}(F),(\lambda,v,s)}$.
\item
The action of terms to an algebra $(A,\tau)$ is inductively defined as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item
For $x_i\in T_{0,(\lambda,v,v(i))}$, $\tau(x_i):\prod_{j\in \lambda}A_{v(j)}\rightarrow A_{v(i)}$ is defined as $(a_j)_{j\in\lambda}\mapsto a_i$.
\item
If $t=(f,(t_i)_{i\in \mathrm{ar}(F)})$,
$\tau(t):\prod_{j\in \lambda}A_{v(j)}\rightarrow A_{{\rm cod}(f)}$ is defined as
\[
(a_j)_{j\in\lambda}\mapsto \tau(f)(\tau(t_i)(a_j)_{j\in\lambda})_{i\in\mathrm{ar}(F)}.
\]
\end{itemize}
\item
For $s\in S$, An $s$-sorted identity is a pair of two $s$-valued terms.
The tuple $(t_1,t_2)$ is usually denoted by
$t_1=t_2$ when it is considered as an identity.
A relation $(A,\tau) \models t_1=t_2$ between an algebra $(A,\tau)$ and 
an equation $t_1=t_2$ is defined by $\tau(t_1)=\tau(t_2)$.
\item
An equational theory is a set of identities.
An algebra $A$ and an equational theory $E$,
$A\models E$ means $A\models e$ for all $e\in E$.
A pair $(F,E)$ of type $F$ and equational theory $E$ is called a 
type with equational theory.
\item
A class $\mathcal{V}$ of $F$-algebras is said a variety if there exists
an equational theory $E$ such that \mbox{$\mathcal{V}=\{A\mid A\models E\}$}.
The variety of $F$-algebras defined by $E$ is denoted by $\mathcal{V}_{(F,E)}$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.raw_latex:
Let $S$ and $\kappa$ be cardinals.
An $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone $M$ is a many-sorted algebra
satisfying the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item
(Sort) The set of all sorts of $M$ consists of tuples $(\lambda,v,s)$,
where $\lambda<\kappa$ is a cardinal, $v:\lambda\rightarrow S$ and $s\in S$.
\item
(Operation) $M$ has the following two types of operations:
\begin{itemize}
\item
(Projection) For $\lambda<\kappa$, $v:\lambda\rightarrow S$ and $i\in \lambda$,
$M$ has a nullary operation $\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}\in M_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}$.
\item
(Composition) For $\lambda_k<\kappa, v_k:\lambda_k\rightarrow S$ ($k=1,2$) and $s\in S$,
$M$ has an operation 
\[
c_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s),(\lambda_2,v_2)}:
  M_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}\times \prod_{i\in\lambda_1}M_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}
  \rightarrow M_{(\lambda_2,v_2,s)}
\]
\end{itemize}
\item
(Axiom) $M$ satisfying the following equations:
\begin{itemize}
\item
(Associativity) For $\lambda_k<\kappa,v_k:\lambda_k\rightarrow S$ ($k=1,2,3$) and $s\in S$,
\begin{align*}
&c_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s),(\lambda_3,v_3)}(x,
  (c_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i)),(\lambda_3,v_3)}(y_i,(z_{j})_{j\in\lambda_2}))_{i\in\lambda_1})\\
=&
c_{(\lambda_2,v_2,s),(\lambda_3,v_3)}
(c_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s),(\lambda_2,v_2)}(x,(y_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}),
  (z_j)_{j\in\lambda_2}).
\end{align*}
\item
(Outer identity law) For $\lambda_k<\kappa,v_k:\lambda_k\rightarrow S$ ($k=1,2$)
and $i_0\in\lambda_1$
\[
c_{(\lambda_1,v_1,v_1(i_0)),(\lambda_2,v_2)}
(\pi_{(\lambda_1,v_1,i_0)},(x_i)_{i\in\lambda_1})
=x_{i_0}.
\]
\item
(Inner identity law) For $\lambda<\kappa,v:\lambda\rightarrow S$ and $s\in S$, 
\[
c_{(\lambda,v,s),(\lambda,v)}(x,(\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)})_{i\in\lambda})
=x.
\]
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

A tuple (A,tau) is said an M-algebra if the following conditions hold: item A=(A_s)_sin S is an S-indexed family of sets. item tau=(tau_(lambda,v,s)) is a family of mappings, where (lambda,v,s) runs all tuples that satisfy lambda<kappa, v:lambda rightarrow S and sin S, and tau_(lambda,v,s) is defined on M_(lambda,v,s) and tau_(lambda,v,s)(f) is a mapping prod_iinlambdaA_v(i)rightarrow A_s for each fin M_(lambda,v,s). item For fin M_(lambda_1,v_1,s), (g_i)_iinlambda_1in prod_iinlambda_1M_(lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i)) and (a_j)_jinlambda_2inprod_jinlambda_2A_v_2(j), the following equation holds: \[ tau_(lambda_2,v_2,s)(c_(lambda_1,v_1,s),(lambda_2,v_2)(f,(g_i)_iinlambda_1))(a_j)_jinlambda_2 =tau_(lambda_1,v_1,s)(f)(tau_(lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))(g_i)(a_j)_jinlambda_2)_iinlambda_1. \] The class of all M-algebras is denoted by V(M). Let $S$ and $\kappa$ be a cardinals, $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone.
A tuple $(A,\tau)$ is said an $M$-algebra if the following conditions hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ is an $S$-indexed family of sets.
\item
$\tau=(\tau_{(\lambda,v,s)})$ is a family of mappings, where $(\lambda,v,s)$ runs
all tuples that satisfy $\lambda<\kappa$, $v:\lambda \rightarrow S$ and $s\in S$,
and $\tau_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is defined on $M_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ and
$\tau_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f)$ is a mapping $\prod_{i\in\lambda}A_{v(i)}\rightarrow A_s$
for each $f\in M_{(\lambda,v,s)}$.
\item
For $f\in M_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}$,
$(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}\in \prod_{i\in\lambda_1}M_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}$
and $(a_j)_{j\in\lambda_2}\in\prod_{j\in\lambda_2}A_{v_2(j)}$,
the following equation holds:
\[
\tau_{(\lambda_2,v_2,s)}(c_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s),(\lambda_2,v_2)}(f,(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}))(a_{j})_{j\in\lambda_2}
=\tau_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}(f)(\tau_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}(g_i)(a_j)_{j\in\lambda_2})_{i\in\lambda_1}.
\]
\end{itemize}
The class of all $M$-algebras is denoted by $\mathcal{V}(M)$.
The category of $M$-algebras, that is, the class of objects is $\mathcal{V}(M)$
and the set of morphisms $A$ to $B$ is the set of all homomorphisms $A\rightarrow B$,
is denoted by $\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(M))$.

Let $S$ be a cardinal, $(F,E)$ be an $S$-sorted type with equational theory.
Let $\kappa>S$ be an infinite cardinal.
We define the $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone of $F$ modulo $E$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The underlying set of a sort $(\lambda,v,s)$
is $T_{(\lambda,v,s)}/\mathclose\sim_E$ where
$T_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is the set of all $(\lambda,v)$-ary $s$-valued terms of $F$.
The equivalence $t_1\sim_E t_2$
is defined by the condition
\[
``A\models E\Rightarrow A\models t_1=t_2\text{ for all }
F\text{-algebra }A".
\]
\item
Fundamental operations are defined as
\begin{align*}
\pi_i:=&x_i/\mathclose \sim_E, \\
c(t/\mathclose\sim_E,(u_i/\mathclose\sim_E)_{i\in\lambda})
:=&(t\circ (u_i)_{i\in \lambda})/\mathclose\sim_E.
\end{align*}
This clone is denoted by ${\cal M}_{\kappa}(F,E)$, or 
${\cal M}_\kappa(\mathcal{V}_{(F,E)})$ by using the variety $\mathcal{V}_{(F,E)}$
defined by the equational theory $E$.
\end{itemize}

Let $S$ be a non-zero cardinal, $\kappa>S$ be an infinite cardinal.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If $\mathcal{V}$ is an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary variety, then
the clone ${\cal M}_\kappa(\mathcal{V})$ of terms of $\mathcal{V}$ is
an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone.
\item
For an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone $M$,
there exists an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary variety $\mathcal{V}$
such that ${\cal M}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{V})$ is isomorphic to $M$.
\item
Let $\kappa'>\kappa$ be a cardinal,
$\mathcal{V}_1,\mathcal{V}_2$ be $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary varieties.
Then ${\cal M}_{\kappa'}(\mathcal{V}_1){\simeq}{\cal M}_{\kappa'}(\mathcal{V}_2)$ if and only if
${\cal M}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{V}_1){\simeq}{\cal M}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{V}_2)$.
\end{enumerate}

For simplification, we use, for example, the following variable notations through this paper:
\begin{itemize}
\item
In the case $\lambda$ is finite, the sort $(\lambda,v,s)$ of many-sorted clone is denoted by $(v(0),\dots,v(\lambda-1))\rightarrow s$.
The case $\lambda=1$, $(1,v,s)$ is denoted by $v(0)\rightarrow s$.
The case $v$ is constant mapping, $v(i)=t$ for all $i$, $(n,v,s)$ is denoted by $nt\rightarrow s$.
\item
The composition operation $c$ of a clone is sometimes 
written as a composition of mappings.
For example, $c(x,(y_i)_{i\in\lambda})$ is denoted by
$x\circ(y_i)_{i\in\lambda}$ or $x(y_i)_{i\in \lambda}$.
\item
we write $(b,(a_s)_{s\in S\setminus\{s_0\}})$ the tuple $(x_s)_{s\in S}$ such that
$x_{s_0}=b$ and $x_s=a_s$ for $s\in S$.
The notation $((a_s)_{s\in T},(b_s)_{s\in S\setminus T})$ means the tuple $(x_s)_{s\in S}$
such that $x_s=a_s$ if $s\in T$ and $x_s=b_s$ if $s\in S\setminus T$.
\item
If we write $\pi_{(X,v,x)}\in M_{(X,v,s)}$,
where $M$ is an $S$-sorted clone, $X$ is a set, $v:X\rightarrow S$, $s\in S$ and $x\in X$,
we implicitly fix a bijection $\varphi:X\rightarrow |X|$ and
$M_{(X,v,s)}$ is identified with $M_{(|X|,v\circ\varphi^{-1},s)}$ and
$\pi_{(X,v,x)}$ means
$\pi_{(|X|,v\circ \varphi^{-1},\varphi(x))}$.






\end{itemize}

\label{pure-set}

\mbox{}
\begin{enumerate}
\item
A family $(A_s)_{s\in S}$ of sets said to be pure
if one of the following conditions holds:
One condition is $A_s=\emptyset$ for all $s\in S$.
The other is $A_s\neq \emptyset$ for all $s\in S$.
\item
Let $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ and $B=(B_s)_{s\in S}$ be pure sets.
A morphism $f:A\rightarrow B$ of pure sets is a tuple $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}$ such that
$f_s:A_s\rightarrow B_s$ for all $s\in S$.
\item
A category ${\textbf{{\rm Set}}}^S$ of $S$-sorted pure sets is the category that the class of objects consists of all $S$-sorted pure sets
and the set of morphisms from a pure set $A$ to a pure set $B$ is
the set of all morphisms of pure sets $A\rightarrow B$.
\end{enumerate}

The category ${\textbf{{\rm Set}}}^S$ is categorically equivalent to the category ${\cal D}_S$
via the following categorical equivalence $\varphi$:
\begin{itemize}
\item
(Objects correspondence) For $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}\in {\textbf{{\rm Set}}}^S$, 
$\varphi(A)$ is the following diagonal algebra:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The underlying set is the product set $\prod_{s\in S}A_s$.
\item
For $(x_{s,t})_{t\in S}\in \prod_{t\in S}A_t$ ($s\in S$), the value
of $d$ is defined as
\[
d((x_{s,t})_{t\in S})_{s\in S}:=(x_{s,s})_{s\in S}.
\]
\end{itemize}
\item
(Morphism correspondence)
For a morphism $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}:(A_s)_{s\in S}\rightarrow (B_s)_{s\in S}$ of pure set,
the corresponding homomorphism $\varphi(f):\varphi((A_s)_{s\in S})\rightarrow \varphi((B_s)_{s\in S})$
is defined by $(x_s)_{s\in S}\mapsto (f_s(x_s))_{s\in S}$.
\end{itemize}

\label{homog-clone}
Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone.
A single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone ${\rm H}(M)$ defined as follows is
said a homogenization of $M$:
\begin{itemize}
\item (Underlying set)
For a cardinal $\lambda<\kappa$, the underlying set ${\rm H}_\lambda(M)$ of a sort $\lambda$
(the sort corresponding to all $\lambda$-ary terms) consists of all tuple
$(f_s)_{s\in S}$, where $f_s\in M_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,s)}$.
Here, and through this paper, the symbol $p_2$ is used for the second projection
of a product set.
(In this case, $p_2$ is the mapping $(i,s')\mapsto s'$ from $\lambda\times S$ to $S$.)
\item (Projection) The nullary operation $\pi_{(\lambda,i)}\in {\rm H}_\lambda(M)$ corresponds to
$\lambda$-ary $i$-th projection is define as
\[
\pi_{(\lambda,i)}:=(\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,s))})_{s\in S}.
\]
\item (Composition)
For $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}\in {\rm H}_{\lambda_1}(M)$ and
$g_i=(g_{i,s})_{s\in S}\in {\rm H}_{\lambda_2}(M)$ ($i\in \lambda_1$)
the composition is defined as
\[
c(f,(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}):=(c(f_s,(g_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda_1\times S}))_{s\in S}.
\]
\end{itemize}

\label{many-single}
Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, $A,B$ be $M$-algebras,
and $\varphi:A\rightarrow B$ be a homomorphism of $M$-algebras.
Then ${\rm H}(\varphi):(a_s)_{s\in S}\mapsto (\varphi_s(a_s))_{s\in S}$ is a
homomorphism ${\rm H}(A)\rightarrow {\rm H}(B)$ of ${\rm H}(M)$-algebras.
Furthermore, the following correspondence ${\rm H}$ is a functor from the
category $\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(M))$ of $M$-algebras to the category $\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M)))$
of ${\rm H}(M)$-algebras:
\begin{itemize}
\item
(Object correspondence) $A\mapsto {\rm H}(A)$.
\item
(Morphism correspondence) $\varphi\mapsto {\rm H}(\varphi)$.
\end{itemize}

\]
hold for all homomorphisms $\psi,\varphi$ that ${\rm cod}(\varphi)={\rm dom}(\psi)$.

Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clone.
Assume $d\in {\rm H}_S(M)$ and $e_s\in {\rm H}_1(M)$ ($s\in S$)
be terms satisfying the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$d$ is defined as $d=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))})_{s\in S}$.
(Intuitively, the term operation of $d$ acts as
\[
A^S\ni ((a_{s,t})_{t\in S})_{s\in S}\mapsto (a_{s,s})_{s\in S}\in A
\]
for each ${\rm H}(M)$-algebra $A$.)
\item
Each term $e_s$ satisfies follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$e_s\circ(\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id}_S,s)},(x_u)_{u\in S\setminus\{s\}})=e_s$
(Intuitively, the value of term operation $e_s(a_u)_{u\in S}$
depends only on $s$-component $a_s$.)
\item
If $e_s=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}$, where $e_{s,t}\in M_{(S,\mathrm{id}_S,t)}$,
then $e_{s,s}=\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id}_S,s)}$.
(Intuitively, the value $e_{s,s}(a_u)_{u\in S}$ of $s$-component
is $a_s$.)
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
Then the following equations hold in ${\rm H}(M)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$e_s\circ d=e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}$.
\item
$d\circ(e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)})_{s\in S}=d$.
\item
$d\circ (\pi_{(S,0)})_{s\in S}=\pi_{(S,0)}$, where $0\in S$.
\end{enumerate}

\label{diagonal-pair}
Let $C$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone.
The tuple $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})\in C_S\times C_1{}^S$ is 
said an $S$-ary diagonal pair of $C$ if the following equations holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$e_{s}\circ d=\pi_{(S,s)}$ for all $s\in S$.
\item
$d(e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)})_{s\in S}=d$.
\item
$d(\pi_{(S,0)})_{s\in S}=\pi_{(S,0)}$ for $0\in S$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.raw_latex:
The matrix product $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$ of a family of
idempotent retracts $(e_s(C))_{s\in S}$ is defined as
the following $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone:
\begin{itemize}
\item (Underlying set)
The underlying set $(\boxtimes_{s\in S}e(C))_{\lambda}$ of the sort $\lambda<\kappa$ is 
\[
\{(f_s/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda})_{s\in S}\in (C_{\lambda\times S}/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda})^S
 \mid \forall s\in S;e_sf_s=f_s\}, 
\]
where the equivalence $\sim_\lambda$ is defined as
\[
f\sim_{\lambda} g:\Longleftrightarrow
f\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}
=g\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}.
\]
\item (Projection)
The $\lambda$-ary $i$-th projection $\pi_{(\lambda,i)}$ is defined by
$(e_s\circ \pi^{C}_{\lambda\times S,(i,s)}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_\lambda)_{s\in S}$,
where $\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,s))}^C$ is the $\lambda\times S$-ary $(i,s)$-th
projection constant of $C$.
\item (Composition)
For $f=(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_1})_{s\in S}\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e(C))_{\lambda_1}$
and $g_i=(g_{i,s}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2})_{s\in S}\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e(C))_{\lambda_2}$
($i\in\lambda_1$), the composition is defined by
\[
c(f,(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1})
:=(c^C(f_s,(g_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda_1\times S})\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2})_{s\in S},
\]
where $c^C$ is the composition operation of $C$.

Let $C$ be a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, $A$ be a $C$-algebra.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
Let $e\in C_1$ be an idempotent element.
The idempotent retract (in literature e.g. \cite{Iza},\cite{Kea},
this is referred as a neighbourhood) of 
$A$ by $e$, denoted by $e(A)$, is defined as the following $e(C)$-algebra:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The underlying set is $e(A)=\{e(a)\mid a\in A\}$.
\item
The action of $f\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_\lambda\in (e(C))_{\lambda}$ is
$(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\mapsto f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}$.
\end{itemize}
\item
Let $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ be a family of idempotent elements of $C$.
The matrix product $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(A)$ is defined as
the following $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$-algebra:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The underlying set is $\prod_{s\in S}e_s(A)$.
\item
The action of
$(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_\lambda)_{s\in S}\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_\lambda$ is
\[
((a_{i,t})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\mapsto 
(f_s(a_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{s\in S}.
\]
\end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

Let $C$ be a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone and $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ be a
family of idempotent elements of $C$.
Let $A$ and $B$ be $C$-algebras, $\varphi:A\rightarrow B$ be a homomorphism of $C$-algebras.
Then the mapping \mbox{$\tilde{\varphi}:\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(A)\rightarrow \boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(B)$}
defined as $(a_s)_{s\in S}\mapsto (\varphi(a_s))_{s\in S}$ is a homomorphism of
$\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$-algebras.
Furthermore, the (pair of) correspondence $A\mapsto \boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(A)$ and
$\varphi\mapsto \tilde{\varphi}$ is a functor $\mathcal{V}(C)\rightarrow \mathcal{V}(\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))$.

Let $f=(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_\lambda)_{s\in S}\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_{\lambda}$ and
$a_{i}=(a_{i,s})_{s\in S}\in \boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(A)$ for $i\in\lambda$.
Then
\begin{align*}
\tilde{\varphi}(f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda})
&=(\varphi(f_s(a_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}))_{s\in S}\\
&=(f_s(\varphi(a_{i,t}))_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{s\in S}\\
&=f(\tilde{\varphi}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}.
\end{align*}
The correspondence $\varphi\mapsto \tilde{\varphi}$ clearly preserves
identity morphisms and composition.
Thus the correspondence is a functor.

Suppose $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of $C$.
We define $\varphi_\lambda:C_\lambda\rightarrow (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_\lambda$
as
\[
\varphi_\lambda:f\mapsto 
 (e_s\circ f\circ 
  (d\circ(\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})
   _{i\in\lambda}/\mathclose\sim_\lambda)_{s\in \lambda}.
\]
Note that $\varphi_{\lambda}(f)\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_\lambda$
follows from $e_s\circ e_s=e_s$.

We prove injectivity of $\varphi_\lambda$.
Let $f,g\in C_\lambda$ and assume $\varphi_\lambda(f)=\varphi_\lambda(g)$,
namely, assume the equality
\begin{align*}
 &e_sf\circ(d\circ(e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\\
=&e_sf\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}
  \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\
=&e_sg\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}
  \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\
=&e_sg\circ(d\circ(e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}
\end{align*}
hold for all $s\in S$. Then
\begin{align*}
f
=&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ f\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}\\
=&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ f\circ 
  (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\\
=&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ f\circ 
  (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}
  \circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\
=&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ f\circ 
  (d\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}
  \circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\
=&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ g\circ 
  (d\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}
  \circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\



=&g.
\end{align*}

Next, we prove surjectivity of $\varphi_\lambda$.
Let $(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda})_{s\in S}\in(\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_\lambda$.
We define $\tilde{f}\in C_\lambda$ as
\[
\tilde{f}:=d\circ (f_s)_{s\in S}\circ 
(e_t\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}.
\]
Then
\begin{align*}
\varphi_{\lambda}(\tilde{f})
=&\left(e_sd\circ (f_t)_{t\in S}
  \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}
  \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda}\right)_{s\in S}\\
=&\left(e_sf_s
  \circ (e_td\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda}\right)_{s\in S}\\
=&\left(f_s
  \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda}\right)_{s\in S}\\
=&(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda})_{s\in S}.
\end{align*}

Finally, we prove $\varphi=(\varphi_{\lambda})_{\lambda<\kappa}$ is a homomorphism.
Let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2<\kappa$ and $f\in C_{\lambda_1}$,
$g_i\in C_{\lambda_2}$ for $i\in\lambda_1$.
Then
\begin{align*}
&\varphi_{\lambda_2}(f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1})\\
=&\left(e_s f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}
  \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{s\in S}\\
=&\left(e_sf\circ (d\circ (g_i)_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1}
  \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{s\in S}\\
=&\left(e_s f\circ (d\circ (e_ug_i)_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1}
  \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{s\in S}\\
=&\left(e_s f\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_1\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1}
  \circ (e_ug_i)_{(i,u)\in\lambda_1\times S}
  \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{s\in S}\\
=&\left(e_s f\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_1\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_1}\right)_{s\in S}
  \circ \left(e_ug_i
  \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{(i,u)\in \lambda_1\times S}\\
=&\varphi_{\lambda_1}(f)\circ (\varphi_{\lambda_2}(g_i))_{i\in\lambda_1}.
\end{align*}

Let $C$ be a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone and ${(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$, ${(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$
be diagonal pairs of $C$.
Then $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$ is isomorphic to  $C_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$ via an isomorphism
$\varphi=(\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)})$ where
\[
\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}:C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}\ni f/\mathclose \sim\mapsto 
e'_sf(e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}/\mathclose\sim'
\in C_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}.
\]
Here, $\sim$ and $\sim'$ are equivalences defined as
\begin{align*}
f\sim g:\Longleftrightarrow 
  f\circ (e_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}
 =g\circ (e_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda},\\
f\sim' g:\Longleftrightarrow 
  f\circ (e'_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}
 =g\circ (e'_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}.
\end{align*}

Well-definedness of $\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ directly follows from the definition.

Let $\psi_{(\lambda,v,s)}:C_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}\rightarrow
C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}$ be the mapping
$g/\mathclose\sim'\mapsto e_sg(e'_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}/\mathclose\sim$.
Then by the previous lemma,
\begin{align*}
\psi_{(\lambda,v,s)}\circ \varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f/\mathclose\sim)
=&\left(e_se'_sf(e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}
  \circ(e'_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\
=&\left(e_sf(e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\
=&f/\mathclose\sim.
\end{align*}
By the same way,
$\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}\circ \psi_{(\lambda,v,s)}=
\mathrm{id}_{C_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}}$
holds. Thus $\psi_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is the inverse of $\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}$.
Particularly, $\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is bijective.


We prove $\varphi$ is compatible with $S$-sorted clone operations.
Let $\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}=e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)}/\mathclose\sim$ be the
$(\lambda,v)$-ary $i$-th projection of $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$.
Then
\[
\varphi_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}(\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)})
=\left(e'_{v(i)}e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)}(e_{v(j)}\pi_{(\lambda,j)})_{j\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim'
=(e'_{v(i)}e_{v(i)}\circ e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})/\mathclose\sim'
=e'_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)}/\mathclose\sim'
\]
by the previous lemma.
It is the $(\lambda,v)$-ary $i$-th projection of $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$.

Next, let $\lambda_k<\kappa$, $v_k:\lambda_k\rightarrow S$ ($k=1,2$),
$s\in S$ and 
\[
f/\mathclose\sim\in C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda_1,v_1,s)},
g_i/\mathclose\sim\in C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}
\]
for $i\in\lambda_1$.
Then
\begin{align*}
&\varphi_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}(f/\mathclose\sim)
 \circ (\varphi_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}(g_i/\mathclose\sim))_{i\in\lambda_1}&\\
=&(e'_sf(e_{v_1(i)}\pi_{(\lambda_1,i)})_{i\in\lambda_1}/\mathclose\sim)\circ 
 (e'_{v_1(i)}g_i(e_{v_2(j)}\pi_{(\lambda_2,j)})_{j\in\lambda_1}/\mathclose\sim)_{i\in\lambda_1}&\\
=&\left(e'_sf(e_{v_1(i)}e'_{v_1(i)}g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}\circ 
  (e_{v_2(j)}\pi_{(\lambda_2,j)})_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim'&\\
=&\left(e'_sf(e_{v_1(i)}g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}\circ 
  (e_{v_2(j)}\pi_{(\lambda_2,j)})_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim'
  &(\text{Lemma \ref{different-projection}})\\
=&\left(e'_sf(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}\circ 
  (e_{v_2(j)}\pi_{(\lambda_2,j)})_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim'
  &(g_i/\mathclose\sim\in C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})})\\
=&\varphi_{(\lambda_2,v_2,s)}(f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}).&
\end{align*}

By definition of diagonal pair, $(a_s)_{s\in S}\mapsto d(a_s)_{s\in S}$ is 
the inverse mapping of $\nu_A$. Thus $\nu_A$ is bijective.

We prove $\nu_A$ is a homomorphism of $C$-algebras.
Let $f\in C_\lambda$, $\lambda<\kappa$ and $(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\in A^\lambda$.
Then
\begin{align*}
\nu_\lambda(f)(\nu_A(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}
&=(e_sf(d(e_t(a_i))_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda})_{s\in S}\\
&=(e_sf(a_i)_{i\in\lambda})_{s\in S}\\
&=\nu_A(f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}).
\end{align*}
This equation is nothing but the property we should prove.

Next, we prove naturalness of $(\nu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(C)}$.
Let $A,B\in\mathcal{V}(C)$ and $\varphi:A\rightarrow B$ be a homomorphism.
We should the diagram
\[\xymatrix{
A\ar[r]^{\nu_A} \ar[d]_\varphi& {\rm H}(A_d)\ar[d]^{{\rm H}(\varphi_d)}\\
B\ar[r]^{\nu_B} & {\rm H}(B_d)
}\]
commute. For $a\in A$,
\begin{align*}
{\rm H}(\varphi_d)(\nu_A(a))
&={\rm H}(\varphi_d)(e_s(a))_{s\in S}\\
&=(\varphi(e_s(a))_{s\in S}\\
&=(e_s(\varphi(a))_{s\in S}\\
&=\nu_B(\varphi(a))
\end{align*}
holds. It means $(\nu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(C)}$ is a natural transformation.

Let $f\in M_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ and $a_i\in A_{v(i)}$ for $i\in\lambda$.
Then
\begin{align*}
\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f)(\mu_{A,v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}
&=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))})_{i\in\lambda}
(e_{v(i),u}(a_i))_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S}\\
&=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f(e_{v(i),v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\
&=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\\
&=\mu_{A,s}(f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}).
\end{align*}
This equation is nothing but the proposition stated.

We prove $(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation.
Let $A=(A_s)_{s\in S},B=(B_s)_{s\in S}\in \mathcal{V}(M)$ and $\varphi=(\varphi_s)_{s\in S}$
be a homomorphism $A\rightarrow B$.
We prove should the diagram
\[\xymatrix{
A\ar[r]^{\mu_A} \ar[d]_\varphi& ({\rm H}(A))_d\ar[d]^{({\rm H}(\varphi))_d}\\
B\ar[r]^{\mu_B} & ({\rm H}(B))_d
}\]
commute. For $s\in S$ and $a\in A_s$, the equation
\begin{align*}
\mu_{B,s}(\varphi_s(a))
&=(e_{s,t}(\varphi_s(a))_{t\in S}\\
&=(\varphi_t(e_{s,t}(a)))_{t\in S}\\
&={\rm H}(\varphi)(e_{s,t}(a))_{t\in S}\\
&=({\rm H}(\varphi))_{d,s}(\mu_{A,s}(a))
\end{align*}
holds.
This is nothing but $\mu_B\circ \varphi=({\rm H}(\varphi))_d\circ \mu_A$, thus
it is proved that $(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation.

Let $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ be an $S$-sorted algebra.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
A subalgebra of $A$ is an $S$-sorted family $B=(B_s)_{s\in S}$ that satisfies
the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$B_s\subset A_s$ for all $s\in S$.
\item
For $(\lambda,v)$-ary $s$-valued term operation $f$ of $A$ and
$(b_i)_{i\in\lambda}\in \prod_{i\in\lambda}B_{v(i)}$,
$f(b_i)_{i\in \lambda}\in B_s$ holds.
\end{itemize}
The set of all subalgebras of $A$ is denoted by $\mathrm{Sub}(A)$.
\item
A congruence of $A$ is a subalgebra $(\theta_s)_{s\in S}$ of $A^2=(A_s{}^2)_{s\in S}$ such that
$\theta_s$ is an equivalence relation on $A_s$ for each $s\in S$.
The set of all congruences of $A$ is denoted by $\mathrm{Con}(A)$.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sub-con-corresopndence}
Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted clone, $A$ be an $M$-algebra.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If $B=(B_s)_{s\in S}\in \mathrm{Sub}(A)$, then ${\rm H}(B):=\prod_{s\in S}B_s\in \mathrm{Sub}({\rm H}(A))$.
Conversely, Any subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$ is described as in the form
${\rm H}(B)$ by $B\in\mathrm{Sub}(A)$.
\item
If $\theta=(\theta_s)_{s\in S}\in\mathrm{Con}(A)$, then
\[
{\rm H}(\theta):=\prod_{s\in S}\theta_s
:=\{((a_s)_{s\in S},(b_s)_{s\in S})\in ({\rm H}(A))^2\mid
 \forall s\in S;(a_s,b_s)\in\theta_s\} \in\mathrm{Con}({\rm H}(A)).
\]
Conversely, Any congruence of ${\rm H}(A)$ is described as in the form
${\rm H}(\theta)$ by a congruence $\theta\in\mathrm{Con}(A)$.
\item
If $\theta\in \mathrm{Con}(A)$, then ${\rm H}(A/\theta){\simeq} {\rm H}(A)/{\rm H}(\theta)$.
\item
If $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family of $M$-algebras, then
\[
\prod_{i\in I}{\rm H}(A_i){\simeq} {\rm H}\left(\prod_{i\in I} A_i\right).
\]
\end{enumerate}

In such case, the correspondence Bmapsto H(B) between Sub(A) and Sub(H(A)) is bijective. On the other hand, this correspondence may not be bijective if M is not pure. For a simple example, S=2=\0,1\, M be the trivial 2-sorted clone (that is, the 2-sorted clone only consists of projection constants) and A=(A_i)_iin 2=(A_0,A_1), then the both (emptyset,A_1) and (A_0,emptyset) of members of Sub(A) correspond to emptyset=emptysettimes A_1=A_0timesemptyset.

\label{subalgebra-of-pure-algebra}
If $M$ is a pure clone, then the underlying family of sets of any subalgebra of an $M$-algebra $A$ is pure. In such case, the correspondence $B\mapsto {\rm H}(B)$
between $\mathrm{Sub}(A)$ and $\mathrm{Sub}({\rm H}(A))$ is bijective. On the other hand,
this correspondence may not be bijective if $M$ is not pure.
For a simple example, $S=2=\{0,1\}$, $M$ be the trivial $2$-sorted clone
(that is, the $2$-sorted clone only consists of projection constants)
and $A=(A_i)_{i\in 2}=(A_0,A_1)$, then the both $(\emptyset,A_1)$ and $(A_0,\emptyset)$
of members of $\mathrm{Sub}(A)$ correspond to $\emptyset=\emptyset\times A_1=A_0\times\emptyset$.

We show
\begin{equation}\label{varieties-through-homogenization}
{\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathbf{HSP}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))={\rm H}(\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})).
\end{equation}
The second equality is Birkhoff's variety theorem for classes of single-sorted algebras.
The last equality follows from Proposition \ref{sub-con-corresopndence}.

The first equality is proved as follows. 
For $f,g\in {\rm H}_\lambda(M)$, where $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}$, $g=(g_s)_{s\in S}$,
the following equivalence holds:
\begin{align*}
{\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))\models f=g
\Longleftrightarrow& \forall s\in S;\ \mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})\models f_s=g_s\\
\Longleftrightarrow& \forall s\in S;\ \mathcal{K}\models f_s=g_s\\
\Longleftrightarrow& {\rm H}(\mathcal{K})\models f=g\\
\Longleftrightarrow& \mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))\models f=g.
\end{align*}
It means the equational theories defining $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))$ and ${\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))$
coincide with each other.
Therefore, ${\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))$ holds.
By (\ref{varieties-through-homogenization}) and Theorem \ref{main-theorem-categorical-equivalence},
$\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})=\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})$ holds.

Let $A$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary algebra, $\kappa'$ be a cardinal.
A $<\mathclose\kappa'$-ary relational clone of $A$ is the family $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A)=(\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A))_{\mu<\kappa'}$,
where $\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)=\{{\rm H}(B)\mid B\in\mathrm{Sub}(A)\}$,
namely, $\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)$ is the set of all subsets $r$ of
$\left(\prod_{s\in S}A_s\right)^\mu$ that satisfy
\begin{align*}
&f_s\in \mathrm{Clo}_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,s)}(A),(a_{i,j,t})_{(t,j)\in S\times\mu}\in r\ (\text{for }i\in\lambda)\\
\Longrightarrow& (f_s(a_{i,j,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{(s,j)\in S\times\mu}\in r.
\end{align*}
Here, $\mathrm{Clo}_{(\lambda,v,s)}(A)$ is the set of all $(\lambda,v)$-ary $s$-valued term operations of $A$.
A member of $\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)$ is said an $\mu$-ary invariant set of $A$.

Let $S_k$ be a non-zero cardinal, $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal that $S_k<\kappa$ for $k=1,2$.
Let $A_k$ be an $S_k$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary algebra that the clones of term operations are pure for $k=1,2$.
Let $\kappa'$ be an infinite cardinal that satisfies
\[
\lambda<\kappa\ \Longrightarrow |A_1|^\lambda, |A_2|^\lambda <\kappa',
\]
where $|A_k|$ is the product cardinal $\prod_{s\in S_k} |A_{k,s}|$.
Then the following assertions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
There exists a categorical equivalence $\mathcal{V}(A_1)\rightarrow\mathcal{V}(A_2)$ that maps $A_1$ to $A_2$.
\item
The relational clones $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_1)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_2)$.
\end{enumerate}

Let $A$ be an $S$-sorted algebra.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
Let $\theta_s,\eta_s\subset A_s{}^2$.
A relational product $\theta\circ\eta$ of $\theta=(\theta_s)_{s\in S}$ and $\eta=(\eta_s)_{s\in S}$
is defined by sort-wise relational product $(\theta_s\circ\eta_s)_{s\in S}$. 
\item
An algebra $A$ is said congruence  permutable if $\theta\circ\eta=\eta\circ\theta$
for all $\theta,\eta\in\mathrm{Con}(A)$.
\item
A class of algebras $\mathcal{K}$ is said congruence permutable if all members of
$\mathcal{K}$ are congruence permutable.
\end{enumerate}

\label{malcev}
Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted pure clone.
Then the following conditions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\mathcal{V}(M)$ is congruence permutable.
\item
$\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ is congruence permutable.
\item
There exists $p\in {\rm H}_3(M)$, called Mal'cev term, that satisfies
\[
p(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,1)})=\pi_{(3,1)}
,p(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,1)},\pi_{(3,1)})=\pi_{(3,0)},
\]
where $3$ is a three elements set $\{0,1,2\}$.
\item
For each $s\in S$, there exists $p_s\in M_{(3\times S,p_2,s)}$ such that
\begin{align*}
p_s((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S})
=\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))},\\
p_s((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S})
=\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))}.
\end{align*}
\item
For each $s\in S$, there exists $p_s\in M_{3s\rightarrow s}$ such that
\begin{align*}
p_s(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)})
=\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)},\\
p_s(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)})
=\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)}.
\end{align*}
\end{enumerate}

namely, there are three elements $a,b,c$ of sort $s$ such that $\{a,b,c\}$ freely
generates $F$. Let $\theta$ and $\eta$ be congruences of $F$ generated by

Let $S$ be a finite set, $M$ be an $S$-sorted finitary pure clone.
Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\mathcal{V}(M)$ is congruence distributive.
\item
$\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ is congruence distributive.
\item
There are an integer $n\geq 0$ and $d_0,\dots,d_{2n}\in {\rm H}_3(M)$,
we call J\'onsson term of length $n$ in this paper,
that satisfy the following equations:
\begin{align*}
d_0=\pi_{(3,0)},d_{2n}=\pi_{(3,2)}\\
d_{i-1}(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,1)},\pi_{(3,0)})=d_{i}(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,1)},\pi_{(3,0)})
 &\ (1\leq i\leq 2n)\\
d_{2i}(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,2)})=d_{2i+1}(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,2)})
 &\ (0\leq i\leq n-1)\\
d_{2i-1}(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,2)},\pi_{(3,2)})=d_{2i}(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,2)},\pi_{(3,2)})
 &\ (1\leq i\leq n)
\end{align*}
\item
There exists an integer $n\geq 0$ such that, for each $s\in S$, there exist
$d_{s,i}\in M_{(3\times S,p_2,s)}$ ($0\leq i\leq 2n$) that satisfy the following equations:
\begin{align*}
&d_{s,0}=\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,s))},d_{s,2n}=\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(2,s))},&\\
&d_{s,i-1}((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S})&\\
 =&d_{s,i}((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S}),
 &\ (1\leq i\leq 2n)\\
&d_{s,2i}((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(2,t))})_{t\in S})&\\
 =&d_{s,2i+1}((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(2,t))})_{t\in S}),
 &\ (0\leq i\leq n-1)\\
&d_{s,2i-1}((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(2,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(2,t))})_{t\in S})&\\

 &\ (1\leq i\leq n)
\end{align*}
\item
For each $s\in S$, there exist an integer $n\geq 0$ and
$d_{s,i}\in M_{(3\times S,p_2,s)}$ ($0\leq i\leq 2n$) that satisfy
the same equations displayed in the previous condition.
\item
For each $s\in S$, there exist an integer $n\geq 0$ and
$d_{s,i}\in M_{3s\rightarrow s}$ ($0\leq i\leq 2n$) that satisfy the following equations:
\[
\begin{array}{cl}
d_{s,0}=\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},d_{s,2n}=\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,2)},&\\
d_{s,i-1}(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)})

 &(1\leq i\leq n)
\end{array}
\]
\end{enumerate}

\[

\[

\]
The terms $d_{s,i}$ corresponding to $x_i$ satisfy the equations stated in Condition 6.

1. Each $C_n$ has J\'onsson term, thus $\mathcal{V}(C_n)$ is congruence distributive.
Thus,
\[
\mathcal{V}(C)=\mathcal{V}\left(\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}C_n\right){\simeq} \bigotimes_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{V}(C_n)
\]
is congruence distributive. Here, $\otimes_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{V}(C_n)$ denotes
non-indexed product of the family $\{\mathcal{V}(C_n)\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ of varieties.
By Proposition \ref{sub-con-corresopndence}, $\mathcal{V}(C_d)$ also be congruence distributive.

2. If $C$ has J\'onsson term of length $n$, then $C_{n+1}$ also has J\'onsson term of length $n$.
It is verified by the induction on $n$ that this is impossible.

3. It is easily verified that $e_n(C)$ is isomorphic to $C_n$.
Particularly, $e_n(C)$ has J\'onsson term.
These are nothing but the terms of $C_d$ satisfying Condition 6 of the theorem.

4. Let $f\in C_{d,(\aleph_0,v,n)}$, where $v:\aleph_0\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
By the definition of heterogenization, $f$ is represented by $\tilde{f}\in C_{\aleph_0}$
such that $e_n\circ\tilde{f}=\tilde{f}$. This condition implies that
the $n$-th component of $\tilde{f}$ is an element of $C_n$ (it is finitary),
and other components are $u$ (depend no variables).
Therefore, $\tilde{f}$, particularly $f$, is finitary.
